teams.heading: Wainiqolo sets up all three Fiji tries in 23-21 loss to Italy
teams.body: The right wing drove Fiji's attack in Friday's 11th-place final at Twickenham. His long cut-out pass sent Ponipate Loganimasi weaving through for the first try. After the break he put fellow wing Peniasi Dakuwaqa over, then released No. 8 Kitione Salawa in the 55th minute as Fiji overturned a 17-0 deficit to lead 21-20. Caleb Muntz converted all three, but a scrum penalty on the edge of Fiji's 22 let Tommaso Allan kick the winner with 13 minutes left.

lead.why: The match report gives a fresh Fiji angle on the result: Wainiqolo's hand in every try, rather than the pundit verdicts already run.

teams.heading: Borthwick names Marcus Smith and Henry Pollock among All Blacks play-off replacements
teams.body: Steve Borthwick's bench for Saturday's Nations Championship third-place play-off against New Zealand at Twickenham ran Jamie George, Fin Baxter, Will Stuart, George Martin, Ben Curry, Pollock, Archie McParland and the Harlequins playmaker, with Fin Smith starting at fly-half and Maro Itoje captaining the side. England reached the play-off after winning five of their six pool matches to finish second in the northern hemisphere table, a point behind France, and came in off the previous weekend's 37-12 win over the All Blacks.

lead.why: It is the only new item carrying England's own selection; the Warburton and Jones stories have already run, and the haka fine has no article to source it.

teams.heading: Geoffrey Doumayrou overhauls France's defence with outside-in rush and lineout roles
teams.body: Rugbyrama credits France's new defence coach with the solidity that carried Les Bleus through an injury-hit autumn. His rush defence uses very low body positions that flirt with the limits of the law. Since November the outermost defenders have switched to outside-in framing to hit ball carriers. Every forward now knows his post when defending four-, five-, six- or seven-man lineouts, long a structural weakness. Mickaël Guillard said the squad now knows how many players fold after the first ruck.

lead.why: It is the only new France story that today's editions have not already run, and it explains how Les Bleus defend going into the final.

teams.heading: Sam Prendergast's perfect kicking and cross-kick steer Ireland past Wallabies 38-14
teams.body: The fly-half was flawless off the tee in Friday's win at Allianz Stadium, Twickenham — five conversions and a penalty for 13 points — and his crossfield kick put Rob Baloucoune over for Ireland's third try. Planet Rugby rated Prendergast hugely impressive across November, saying he ran the show and calmly took the right options, while Ireland finished the month with four wins from four. Of the 45 fans in the app who answered after full time, 91% were buzzing.

lead.why: Prendergast's match-winning display is the freshest Ireland story the reader has not yet seen.

teams.heading: Gonzalo Quesada concedes Italy had other options than kicking deep against Fiji
teams.body: Asked about kicking long in the closing stages of Friday's 23-21 win over Fiji at Twickenham, Quesada accepted that, on review, different solutions can be found. At the time, he explained, Italy believed they could win a penalty from the drive. The aim was to keep play out of their own half, trusting the defence and the players on the field to regain possession. Fiji, ahead 21-20 until Tommaso Allan's penalty with 13 minutes left, were held out to the final whistle.

lead.why: The win and Menoncello's surgery have already run; Quesada explaining Italy's late kicking decision is the freshest Italy-specific angle in the coverage.

teams.heading: Finn Russell faces Albornoz again in rematch of Scotland's Córdoba shootout
teams.body: July's meeting in Córdoba produced 12 tries and a 47-38 Scotland win, and Sunday's seventh-place final puts Russell back at fly-half opposite Argentina's Albornoz. Gregor Townsend and Felipe Contepomi are both using the match as a transition towards the 2027 World Cup, where the sides could meet again: under the most widely projected pool outcome, Scotland and Argentina would sit in opposite halves of the knockout bracket, crossing only on the final weekend in Sydney.

lead.why: The only new item, framing the Argentina match as a rematch of July's Córdoba shootout rather than retelling the selection.

teams.heading: Scarlets bring former Wales centre Scott Williams back as academy skills coach
teams.body: The Scarlets confirmed on Thursday that the role runs in partnership with the Coleg Sir Gâr rugby academy, where the two-time Six Nations winner is already attack coach. Williams played 162 matches for the region, helping win the 2017 Pro12 title, and will work across its pathway with those leading the Emerging Player Programme. Academy pathway manager Emyr Phillips said Williams has already worked with Madoc Evans, Jayden Brown and Alfie Luger in the U18 set-up.

lead.why: The Japan selection and result have already run, so the Scarlets appointment of a former Wales centre is the strongest unused Wales-linked event.

teams.heading: Mayco Vivas sent off as France beat 13-man Pumas 45-17 in Paris
teams.body: Hollie Davidson first showed Vivas yellow, upgraded to red on the hour, and Julián Montoya's sin-binning seven minutes later left Argentina two short as France ran in three quick tries in Paris on 21 November. The Pumas had led 10-7 through Justo Piccardo's try despite losing Bautista Delguy early. Boris Wenger also went off, and Santiago Chocobares had withdrawn hours before kick-off. Pablo Matera's interception try was the only consolation after the break.

lead.why: Argentina's own most recent result, with a red card and injuries, and the only fresh Argentina event not already run.

teams.heading: Rugbyrama calls Les Kiss's Wallabies wasteful a year before home World Cup
teams.body: Rugbyrama's Marc Duzan is blunt about Friday's 38-14 fifth-place play-off defeat by Ireland: the Wallabies created countless openings but finished too few, a worrying sign with Australia hosting the World Cup in less than a year. He praised the ball carriers — Joseph Suaalii, Max Jorgensen, Rob Valetini — but found it hard to judge a side whose back line still includes 37-year-old Kurtley Beale. For all their territory and possession, Australia took 23 minutes to score through Jeremy Williams, and that lead lasted three.

lead.why: Freshest Australia-specific item not yet run: a named verdict on the Wallabies' finishing a year out from their home World Cup.

teams.heading: Ben Gunter led Nations Championship pool stage for jackals and dominant tackles
teams.body: Japan's back-rower ended the pool stage with 11 dominant tackles and six jackals, more than any other player in the competition. He also scored one of Japan's three tries in the 28-21 defeat by Wales in Cardiff on 7 November. The set piece held up around him: Japan topped the competition for lineout success at 93.9% and lineout steals with 10. The defence did not — Japan finished the pool stage having conceded 261 points and 40 tries, the worst record in either hemisphere.

lead.why: The only Japan-focused item that hasn't already run; the NEW items are Wales stories.

teams.heading: Jeff Wilson cites fatigue in All Blacks' slide under Dave Rennie
teams.body: Speaking before Saturday's England rematch, the former wing told Sport Nation that Dave Rennie's expansive game is a style not seen since the 2015 World Cup win. He added that a "10-month season" running from February's Super Rugby starts has taken its toll. The approach paid off early, with wins over France, Italy, Ireland and the Springboks, before South Africa took the next three for a 3-1 series. Defeats to Wales and England followed, leaving Rennie with the most losses in a calendar year since 1998.

lead.why: A fresh New Zealand angle, Wilson on fatigue and Rennie's style, distinct from the Umaga defence and 1949 slump pieces already run.

teams.heading: Nigel Owens criticises Rassie Erasmus after World Rugby ban over referee comments
teams.body: Erasmus's latest World Rugby ban follows a press conference the week after the Springboks' defeat by France in Paris, in which he raised match-fixing — not, Owens stresses, as an accusation against officials, but in a way that "certainly put that question out there". The former Test referee, writing for WalesOnline, says Rassie may be unhappy with the process but went about it the wrong way, and that such comments heighten pressure on referees and the abuse that follows. Owens notes Erasmus is now serving a six-match ban.

lead.why: Erasmus's new World Rugby ban over referee comments is fresh coaching news; the selection and Libbok items repeat stories already run.
